title: Unmoved by pain
hook: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai: the one unmoved by pain, pleasure, praise, gold or dust (Sorath M9, ang 633)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world as a wall of sand, and your line: passing, like a dream. Did you pick up the next handful after something fell? If the world is passing, how do you stand in it? Today's hymn answers. Day five hundred eighty-two.
screen: `THE WORLD AS A WALL OF SAND — PASSING, LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Stub your toe on the bed frame at night, and there are two pains. The first is the toe: sharp, real, over in a minute. The second arrives a moment later. Why is the bed there? Why does this always happen to me? I'll be limping all day, I'll be late, everything's ruined. The second pain can last for hours, and it's mostly made of words. A hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur's in Raag Sorath begins with someone who feels the first pain, and doesn't add the second.
screen: `THE STUBBED TOE: THE FIRST PAIN.` → `THE STORY: THE SECOND PAIN.` → `FEELING ONE, NOT ADDING TWO.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai. The one who, in pain, doesn't take pain as pain. Dukh is pain, sorrow. Maanai is to accept, to take something as so. Read carefully, the line doesn't say this person feels nothing. It says that in the middle of dukh, they don't crown it king. Then the hymn draws a whole portrait, in paraphrase. No clinging to pleasure, no fear. Gold and dust seen alike. No slander, no flattery, no greed, attachment or pride. Apart from joy and grief, from honor and dishonor. Hopes and cravings set down. Lust and anger can't touch this person, and in that heart, the hymn says, God lives. Then, who can live like this? Only the one the Guru has blessed, it says, understands the way. And the last line is a picture: Nanak has merged with the Lord, like water with water. Hold onto that image. Pour water into water, and there's no seam. Nothing to defend, nothing to protect. That's the inner reason for the steadiness. The one who is level in all weather isn't gritting their teeth. They've stopped holding themselves apart. Notice too what this isn't. It isn't coldness. Sikh teaching calls for service, sharing and standing up for others, and Sikhs remember the ninth Guru as giving his life to defend other people's freedom of faith. The steadiness here is the calm that lets you act well in a storm, instead of being thrown around by it. Feel the first pain. Don't add the second.
screen: `DUKH MAI DUKH NAHEE MAANAI.` · `GOLD AND DUST SEEN ALIKE.` · `IN THAT HEART, GOD LIVES.` · `WATER MERGED WITH WATER.` · then, large: `LEVEL IN ALL WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay level through one mood. Sit comfortably and check in. What mood is here right now: restless, low, cheerful, tired? Don't change it. Just feel it, the way you'd feel the weather on your face. Then watch for the second layer, the story about the mood. I shouldn't feel this, this always happens, this will last forever. When the story starts, come back to the breath. Let the mood be weather, passing over a steady field. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Unmoved by pain. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn, the one who doesn't take pain as pain is level through every weather, merged with the Lord like water with water.
Your line: level in all weather. Today, when something stings, say: first pain. Then notice if you're adding the second, and put it down. Day five hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath shabad 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai' is sung in kirtan, and Sikhs often recall its portrait of steadiness in times of grief or illness.

myth: the hymn says the steady person feels nothing at all
in pain, they don't take pain as pain; they feel it without crowning it king.
the hymn says that in such a heart, God lives
lust and anger can't touch that person, and in that heart God dwells.
the steadiness here means not caring about others
it's the calm that lets you serve well in a storm.

fork.setup: you stub your toe in the dark, and the mind starts a long story about how everything is ruined. what does the Sorath hymn describe?
options: feeling the pain without taking it as the whole truth.
getting angry at whoever moved the bed.
fork.reveal: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai: in pain, they don't take pain as pain. the hymn ends with Nanak merged with the Lord like water with water.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dukh, pain or sorrow, the first word of the hymn's portrait.

trapdoor: what you thought: unmoved by pain means numb, or tough.
what it means: it means feeling the pain without letting it rule you, steady through pleasure and pain, praise and blame.

what a scholar hears: the hymn closes with the image of water merging with water, a picture of the self losing its separate edge in God, which Guru Tegh Bahadur gives as the reason for the steadiness.

sources.ref: Raag Sorath, Mahalla 9, 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633–634)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut unsourced superlatives ('much-loved', 'one of the loveliest', 'widely sung'); 'Sikhs are told' reworded as what Sikh teaching calls for.

Paraphrase of the full shabad (jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai; sukh sanehu ar bhai nahee jaa kai kanchan maatee maanai; ... kaam krodh jih parsai naahan tih ghat braham nivaasaa; gur kirpaa jih nar kau keenee tih ih jugat pachhaanee; naanak leen bhaio gobind sio jio paanee sang paanee): please confirm wording and Ang.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is given in its traditional Sikh framing (giving his life for others' freedom of faith) and attributed to Sikh memory; a Keeper may want to confirm the wording.
The 'first pain / second pain' frame is an illustration, not a claim about the text's teaching; the reading of 'dukh nahee maanai' as not taking pain as pain should be confirmed.
